V6-Only 2027 Nissan Patrol Starts Production in RHD for the Australian Market
10 photos
Photo: Nissan
As with the Armada and the Infiniti-branded twin for the United States of America, the Patrol for Australia loses V8 oomph in favor of a more sophisticated V6. Gifted with twin snails, the sixer in question is the only engine confirmed for the right-hand-drive 2027 Nissan Armada due in Aussie showrooms next year.
Coming to dealers in the first quarter of 2027, the Y63 in right-hand drive rolls off the Nissan Shatai Kyushu plant's assembly line. Although the Japanese automaker controls nearly half of it, said facility operates as a contract manufacturing base for the Yokohama-based automaker.
Nissan Shatai is used as a contract manufacturer due to legacy, asset efficiency, and manufacturing specialization. For starters, it predates Nissan as an independent car body and train manufacturer before formally joining the Nissan bandwagon in the early 1950s. Nissan does not carry 100 percent of Nissan Shatai's operational costs, and the negotiated master production service agreement allows Nissan to dial back orders without absorbing the full overhead blow.
And finally, Nissan Shantai holds the assembly expertise for body-on-frame models. By keeping body-on-frame designs separate from unibodies from the standpoint of manufacturing, the automaker is further optimizing its global operations. Having cleared all that up, right-hand-drive production was a long time in the making when you remember that the Y63 went official two years ago.
It all started with the Abu Dhabi reveal from September 2024. Two months later, the full-size model was already on sale in Middle Eastern markets. Just like in the US-market Armada, the Patrol uses the Japanese manufacturer's VR35DDTT engine. In Australian specification, it produces a hugely respectable 317 kilowatts and 700 Newton-meters in optimal conditions, namely 425 horsepower and 516 pound-feet when converting from the metric system to American English.
Photo: Nissan The Armada NISMO, which is not part of the Y63 range for the Land Down Under, belts out 460 horsepower. Even in base flavor, the sixer of the right-hand-drive Armada is 19 kilowatts and 140 Newton-meters up on the eight-cylinder lump from before. Speaking of the ol' days, the seven-speed automatic is gone as well. A nine-speed unit now comes by default, with its design based on the 9G-TRONIC from Mercedes-Benz.
Peak torque is delivered earlier in the rev range, helping the Y63 while towing or crawling over broken ground. Its ladder frame is a highlight as well, incorporating larger side members that deliver 40 percent more torsional rigidity when compared to the Y62 generation. Stiffer means the frame resists twisting better when one wheel drops into a rut while the other remains loaded, making the suspension work more predictably off the beaten path.
The stiffer route also means less chassis flex, therefore resulting in NVH improvements over the outgoing Y62. With this new chassis, the Patrol supports up to 3,700 kilograms (8,157 pounds) of maximum braked towing capacity. That puts the Patrol ahead of the Land Cruiser 300's rating, which is 3,500 kilograms (7,716 pounds) in the Australian market.
To qualify for the advertised maximum towing capacity, the Y63 requires the Nissan genuine towbar. Also gifted with more high-strength steel in its body panels, the 2027 model is AUD 2,450 pricier than its forerunner. That is AUD 98,990 sans off-road costs, a starting price that converts to USD 69,035 today.
Six grades join the entry-level Ti, those being the Ti+, Ti-L and Ti-L+, PRO-4X, and Ti-L Reserve. As its name implies, the PRO-4X is the one to have for more serious all-terrain shenanigans. All trims get a two-speed transfer case, an electronic locking rear diff, and electric power steering instead of a hydraulic design. From the Ti-L, the standard suspension is swapped in favor of Intelligent Dynamic Damping.
The system that adjusts damping continuously, regardless of terrain, is only half the story. Both the PRO-4X and the Ti-L Reserve, which are the priciest members of the Aussie range, level up to adaptive air suspension. This suspension design enables the driver to raise the body in off-road mode, while selecting park lowers it for easier loading and entry/exit.
